content.comment_body: Hello, For my project, I need to control three inputs individually so that only one can be active at a time. In my current setup—shown in the screenshot—the inputs go into a user-defined function (UDF) that cycles two outputs based on which input is selected, the required run times, and the activation of a zero position limit switch. Normally, these three inputs are linked to a rotary switch, preventing simultaneous activation; however, for this application I have to use push buttons, which could result in multiple inputs being enabled at once. I'm struggling to find a way to handle this. Ideally, I'd like the program to either block input 2 and 3 when input 1 is high, or have each new input override the status of the other two when it is activated. Any advice is appreciated, as this issue has become quite frustrating.

I tested your suggestion. It somewhat works, but the issue is that when two or more inputs are active, all signals are blocked from passing through. My requirement is: when input 1 is high, it should block input 2 and 3; when input 2 is high, it should block input 1 and 3; and when input 3 is high, it should block input 1 and 2.

Try this version. Just note, if all inputs go high during the same program cycle, the device cannot automatically decide priority—you'll have to define your own priority logic in the program. Regards, [user_name] (translated with Google)

analysis.insight_summary: Users are discussing a control logic scenario involving multiple push-button inputs, where simultaneous activation requires a priority system. The current product and software do not have a built-in way to resolve input conflicts, necessitating custom programming for input prioritization. Users are highlighting both the challenge and the limitation in resolving these cases intuitively within the available software environment.
analysis.user_expectations: The user is looking for an easy solution that allows the system or software to handle input priority automatically—ensuring that only the highest-priority input remains active if multiple are pressed—without requiring extensive manual logic programming.
